title: Nearest-neighbour gates are all you need: High-rate quantum low-density parity-check codes on a planar grid
authors: Boren Gu, Tamas Noszko, Vincent Steffan, Jens Niklas Eberhardt, Joschka Roffe, Jens Eisert, Stergios Koutsioumpas
abstract: High-performance quantum low-density parity-check codes promise substantial reductions in the overhead of fault-tolerant quantum computation, but most constructions require long-range connectivity or qubit shuttling, both of which are difficult to realise in superconducting architectures. Here we introduce a family of quantum low-density parity-check codes that, for the first time, combines planar open-boundary layouts, finite-size advantages over surface codes, and syndrome extraction using only nearest-neighbour gates on a square grid of qubits. The key idea is to generate check-data connectivity dynamically: nearest-neighbour iSWAP walks both define the stabiliser supports and implement their measurement, avoiding the need for a long-range hardware graph. The resulting circuits achieve optimal constant-depth stabiliser measurement, independent of code size, and naturally remove leakage from the system by exchanging the role of check and data qubits at each syndrome extraction round. We find finite-size instances such as a [[323,14,15]] code, whose code-efficiency ratio is nearly an order of magnitude larger than that of rotated surface-code patches. At around 30 circuit qubits per logical qubit, the best directional tile-code layouts reduce the per-logical per-round logical error rate by up to a factor of 1000 relative to rotated surface-code memories. These results show that the advantages of quantum low-density parity-check codes can survive compilation into strictly planar nearest-neighbour circuits, bringing low-overhead fault-tolerant memories closer to near-term hardware.
summary: The paper presents directional tile codes as an advanced alternative to surface codes for fault-tolerant quantum computation on planar grids. By dynamically generating required long-range connections using only nearest-neighbour iSWAP gates, these codes maintain the high efficiency of qLDPC while respecting hardware locality. This breakthrough brings low-overhead quantum memory closer to realization in near-term superconducting devices.
main_problem: To develop high-performance quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes for fault tolerance that overcome the connectivity limitations of surface codes while remaining implementable using only nearest-neighbour gates on planar hardware.
main_result: The proposed directional tile codes successfully translate the efficiency advantages of qLDPC codes into strictly planar, nearest-neighbour circuits, achieving logical error rate reductions up to three orders of magnitude compared to rotated surface codes at comparable overheads.
method: The authors introduce 'directional tile codes' implemented on a square grid. Syndrome extraction is achieved dynamically using only nearest-neighbour iSWAP gates via controlled walks that define both the stabilizer supports and perform the measurement.
model_or_system: The system is modeled as superconducting qubits arranged on a planar square grid, utilizing directional tile codes defined by specific parity conditions (CSS code structure). The implementation relies entirely on local nearest-neighbour interactions (iSWAP gates) for syndrome extraction circuits.
key_observables: Code efficiency ratio ($\eta_{circ}$), per-logical per-round logical error rate ($p_L$), and circuit qubits required per logical qubit ($n_{circ}$).
important_parameters: Physical error rate ($p=0.001$); code size parameters like [[323, 14, 15]]; linear scaling of routing overhead $O(d)$.
main_assumptions: The method assumes that iSWAP interactions can serve as a 'spacetime routing primitive' to define measurements locally; comparisons are made using a uniform circuit-level noise model.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the structure of directional tile codes, compare logical error rates vs. physical overheads against surface codes (Figure 2), and detail the optimization process for routing qubits (Figure 7).
paper_structure: The paper systematically introduces the concept of directional tile codes to address the locality/efficiency trade-off. It details the nearest-neighbour syndrome extraction circuit, analyzes the scaling of physical overheads (routing) through optimization techniques, and finally demonstrates performance gains via error rate comparisons and logical operation implementation.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, hardware-aware pathway to realizing high-rate quantum memory by engineering code structures that respect strict 2D planar connectivity constraints inherent in superconducting architectures.

Spacetime trajectory of the nearest-neighbour CXSWAP syndrome-extraction circuit for a [[18, 2, 𝑑𝑥= 3, 𝑑𝑧= 2]] directional tile code with directional word 𝔇= NESEN. The top-left panel shows the initial layout, while the following panels show the five directional layers N, E, S, E, and N.
